text: Hello everyone, I'm Grace.Welcome back to my lesson.Today we're going to have another reading lesson.Before our lesson, let's get our notebook, worksheet and pens ready.Today we're going to review how to infer or make inferences.Let's start our lesson.A good reader knows how to infer what the writer wants us to know.What is inferring?Inferring means making a conclusion by reasoning.Sometimes we can't directly get to what the writer wants us to know.So we use inferring to connect words and ideas and have a better understanding.It's also called reading between the lines.For example, take a look at this sentence.Oh no, Tommy jumped out of bed.After washing and dressing quickly, he picked up his school bag and hurried out into the street.Here, from Oh no, Tommy jumped out of bed and also washed and dressed quickly and picked up his school bag and hurried out into the street.From all these details, we can see that he was probably late for school.We use the inferring skill in our daily life a lot.For example, if your mom says to you at night, it's already 10 o'clock.You know that she wants you to go to bed.If you say to your mom, what are you doing?It smells so nice.Your mom knows you want to have a taste of the dish she's making.Our teachers use certain types of questions to test if we're good at inferring.This is the first task on your worksheet.Take a moment to take this type of questions.Have you found the questions?Yes, they are.What can you infer from the passage?What probably happened before or after?What would somebody possibly do according to the passage?These questions ask us to infer what probably happened or what the characters in the text would probably do based on the information given in the text.We need our inferring skill to find answers to all those questions.Can you think of more questions testing our inferring skills?Here are some other questions.What can be filled in a blank in this paragraph?Who, what, when, where, how, why?These questions, if the answers can be found in the passage directly, these questions can be targeting inferring skills.Or what would somebody probably say or think or feel according to the passage?So when you see possibly, probably, may, might, you know this is a question to test if we are good at making inferences.I've also found these questions in our examination papers.Remember, if we can't find a direct answer to a specific question from the text, this question is usually a question testing our inferring skills.Then you might ask the most important question.How shall we infer when we read a text?Can you use the same example to draw some tips to help us infer?If we can't find a direct answer to a specific question from the text, this question is usually a question testing our inferring skills.This is your task, too, on your worksheet.Okay, first we read and find what Tom said and did.What did he do?He jumped out of bed.He washed and dressed very quickly.He picked up his school bag and hurried out into the street.From these actions, we know that he was in a hurry.Then we ask ourselves, when do I do everything in such a hurry when I'm late for something?Then we also connect the clue, school bag, to what we know.And we can infer that Tommy might be late for school.We've just used inferring to find the answer.From this example, we can draw two useful tips.First, identify the main idea.Next, we look for context clues like the characters, actions, thoughts, or dialogues.Then we connect these clues with what we already know to find out what the writer wants us to know.It's time for us to put what we've learned into practice.Let's move on to task three.Read the paragraph and then answer a question.Why didn't David like watching TV as much as his brother and sister?Now let's use inferring to answer this question.After reading, we first get the idea that David is different from his brother and sister.Then we find context clues about what David said and did.He answered that he had gone to the library to change the books in the library.He answered that he had gone to the library to change the books he had borrowed.It was the second time he had done so that week.Here so means it was the second time he had borrowed books from the library that week.And he spent several hours in his own room.And the author also told us that he was the best in his class for English.What did David do for hours in his own room?If we connect the library, books, and English together, we can infer that David probably wanted to spend more time reading English books because he preferred reading to watching TV.Here is another one testing how well we make inferences.The writer doesn't tell us how Bob won the race.How did Bob probably win the race?You need to use inferring to answer this question.Pay attention to the context clues.After skimming the whole paragraph, we get to know that it's about a race.We also find that there are several people taking part in the race.谁比其他人跑得更快?在第二条文章中,我们知道我们远离Steve和Jack,而Bob在我们后面。小心,这里有一个重要的信息。Bob,他刚刚在我们后面跑,正在远离我们。那么,他去哪里了?之后,我们发现,Bob在那里。他已经在最后一条路上了,他先来。这里是Bob再次做的。他很努力地遮掩了他的绿色。绿色是一个大白笑。他试图遮掩他的笑容。让我们停下来想想。他应该在遮掩了一些东西。写者还说,我们预期了Steve和Jack在远离冠军前前进入,而不是Bob。因此,他使用了Bob。在捕捉足够的证据后,我们可以做出我们的影响。所以,Bob应该在冠军上骗了。也许,他做了一个短缩。现在我们做影响更好吗?让我们用下一个证据来测试。什么东西能够丰富的?其实,问题是一样的。我们应该怎么做?找出主意和尽可能的证据来帮助您进行影响。《证据》这篇文章是关于写者对冠军的主人所提供的赞赏。《证据》写者还反映道证据是,我不是想让钱破坏那种,而我发现了赞赏不了的资金。这些证据帮助我们找出答案。我拒绝了。我说不,我摔了头,然后对他道歉。这意味着,写者不想要帮助。第四項,這篇文章太小了,整篇文章就在你的工作圖上請在工作圖上寫下整篇文章和問題第四項詞曲
